Genevan Psalter
juh-NEE-vuhn SAWL-ter
n. (a metrical psalter; a worship-book)
From Geneva, the Swiss city of the Reformation, and psalter, a collection of the Psalms set for singing. Compiled under John Calvin between 1539 and 1562, with versifications by Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze and tunes by Louis Bourgeois.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Genevan Psalter is the great fruit of the Reformation’s recovery of congregational praise: the whole book of Psalms put into metre and set to sturdy melodies so that ordinary believers, not a clerical choir, might sing the Word of God back to Him. Calvin held that what God commands in worship He also supplies, and that the Psalter is the inspired hymnbook God Himself gave His Church. Thus the regulative principle of worship—that the Lord be approached only as He has appointed in Scripture—found living form: psalm-singing by the gathered people. Calvin called the Psalms “an anatomy of all the parts of the soul,” for there is no affection a man may feel that is not mirrored there, and so he labored to give every congregation the entire 150 in their own tongue. The tunes were dignified and unadorned, the harmonies kept simple lest the music eclipse the words. From Geneva this pattern spread through the Reformed and Presbyterian churches and shaped English and Scottish psalmody for generations. The Psalter teaches us that acceptable worship is not invented by men but received from God, that praise is to be God-centered and Word-saturated, and that the humblest believer’s voice, lifted in the words of David and ultimately of Christ, is a sweeter offering than any contrivance of human ingenuity. It is the regulative principle made audible.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A metrical version of the Psalms compiled at Geneva under Calvin for congregational singing, foundational to Reformed worship.

GENEVAN PSALTER, n. From Geneva and psalter; the book of the Psalms versified and set to music under John Calvin, 1539–1562.

A collection of all 150 Psalms in metre, designed for the unaccompanied singing of the whole congregation.

The chief practical embodiment of the principle that God is to be worshiped only as He has commanded in His Word.

Its tunes, plain and grave, were intended to carry the inspired text without overshadowing it.

As the Psalmist enjoins, “Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works” (Psalm 105:2).

📖 Key Scripture

Ps 105:2 — "Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works."

Ps 95:1 — "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation."

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Psalter’s God-given pattern of reverent, Word-filled praise is displaced wherever worship is reshaped to please the worshiper rather than the Lord.

expand to see more

The chief modern corruption is the inversion of worship from a God-appointed offering into a self-centered “worship experience,” engineered for emotional effect and measured by how it makes the audience feel. The Genevan Psalter rebukes this at the root: Calvin asked not what men preferred but what God commanded, and answered with the inspired Psalms sung plainly by all. When the words of Scripture give way to vague sentiment and the tune is built to overpower rather than to serve the text, the creature has begun to dictate the terms of his approach to the Creator.

A related error treats the regulative principle as a relic and worship as a field for unbounded invention. But Nadab and Abihu fell for offering strange fire the Lord commanded not (Leviticus 10:1–2), and our Lord rebuked worship taught by the commandments of men (Mark 7:7). To recover the Psalter is to recover the conviction that God is jealous for His own praise, that He has not left us to guess how to draw near, and that the surest worship is His own Word returned to Him in song.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Psalter grows from Calvin’s conviction that God supplies the very words of acceptable praise.

expand to see more

Calvin’s 1539 Strasbourg edition set the first psalms to metre and tune.

Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze versified the French text.

Louis Bourgeois composed many of the grave, memorable melodies.

The completed 1562 edition contained all 150 Psalms.

Its pattern shaped Scottish, Dutch, and English Reformed psalmody for centuries.

Usage

"“The congregation rose and sang from the Genevan Psalter, every voice carrying the words of David.”"

"“Calvin grounded the Genevan Psalter in the regulative principle of worship.”"

"“The Old Hundredth descends from a tune of the Genevan Psalter.”"
